title.en: Expressions for patterns and calendar relationships

text.en: Mina lists three dates that fall in the same column of a calendar. She wants a rule that works for any starting date in that column.

A letter can stand for the first value in a pattern. When a calendar date is n, the same weekday one week later is n + 7, as long as both dates are in the same month. For a repeating increase, multiply the step size by the number of steps taken. Substitute values to check whether a rule fits the situation.
Use n for the first date so the rule can work for more than one starting value.
Move one row down the same calendar column. The value grows by seven.
Two steps add seven twice, so the expression is n plus fourteen.
Substitute eight. The next two dates on the same weekday are fifteen and twenty-two.

problem.en: Can three same-weekday dates in one month be 9, 16 and 23?

text.en: Let n = 9, then find n + 7 and n + 14.

why.en: Calendar rows for the same weekday are seven days apart.
The three dates follow the same-column pattern.

prompt.en: Explain why the fourth date in the same column is n + 21.

requiredIdeas.en: There are three steps from the first date.

points.en: Represent a starting value with a letter.
Use substitution to check a relationship.
